title: Why Multi-Bank Complexity Is Killing Your Target Close Date
summary: Organizations with 50 banking relationships carry close timelines days longer than necessary because data collection, not accounting complexity, consumes the first half of the close window.
body_markdown:
Ask a CFO how long the monthly close takes and the answer is usually a number: 5 days, 7 days, 10 days. Ask the controller what actually happens inside those days and a different picture emerges. At organizations managing 50 banking relationships, the month end close timeline is not a single process with a clean start and finish. It is a series of dependent phases where each one waits for the one before it, and the first phase is entirely controlled by external parties. Our team estimates that organizations with 50 or more banking partners carry close timelines 3 to 5 days longer than organizations with fewer than 10, not because of accounting complexity but because of data collection overhead.


## **Days 1 Through 3: Waiting and Collecting**


The first days of the close at a multi-bank organization are not close days. They are gathering days. Bank statements arrive on different schedules. Some are available on the first business day. Others post on day two or three. A handful require manual downloads from portals because automated delivery was never established. The controller tracks which statements have arrived and which have not, often in a spreadsheet that serves as the unofficial project management tool for the entire close. Until the last critical statement lands, downstream work either stalls or proceeds on incomplete data with the expectation of rework.


The close calendar says day one. The data says not yet.


## **Days 3 Through 5: Reconciliation Under Pressure**


Once statements arrive, reconciliation begins. At 50 banks, this means matching transactions across dozens of accounts, each with its own format, its own transaction coding, and its own quirks. Multi-bank accounting at this scale produces a high volume of exceptions: timing differences, format mismatches, and items that require manual investigation. We often see controllers carry 50 to 150 reconciliation exceptions per close cycle across a 50-bank portfolio, with 20% to 30% requiring cross-functional input from AP, treasury, or property management to resolve.


The reconciliation phase compresses into whatever time remains after collection. If statements took three days to gather, reconciliation gets squeezed into two.


## **Days 5 Through 7: Journals, Adjustments, and the Cascade**


Once reconciliation clears, journal entries post. Adjustments follow. Intercompany eliminations require both sides to be reconciled before they can finalize. At multi-entity organizations, a single entity with an unresolved bank reconciliation can hold open the consolidated close. The cascade is rigid: nothing downstream can finalize until everything upstream is complete. A late statement from one bank on day three becomes an unresolved exception on day five, which becomes a delayed journal entry on day six, which becomes a missed close target on day seven.


One late bank statement can hold open the entire consolidated close.


## **Where Financial Close Benchmarks Mislead**


Most financial close benchmarks report averages across industries and company sizes without accounting for banking relationship count. A 5-day close benchmark may be realistic for an organization with 5 banking partners and centralized data. It is not realistic for an organization managing 50 banks across 30 entities with manual statement collection and per-bank reconciliation workflows. CFOs benchmarking their close against industry averages without adjusting for multi-bank complexity are measuring against a standard that does not reflect their operating environment.


The more useful benchmark is internal: how many days of the close timeline are consumed by data collection versus actual accounting work? If collection takes more than 30% of the total window, the timeline problem is upstream of the close itself.


## **Compressing the Timeline at the Source**


Adding headcount to the reconciliation phase does not solve a collection problem. Extending the close window does not solve a data availability problem. The leverage is in eliminating the gathering phase entirely. A platform like Arpari retrieves bank statements across all 50 banking partners automatically, normalizes formats, and delivers a complete dataset on day one. Reconciliation starts immediately instead of waiting for the last statement to arrive. Exceptions surface earlier, which means cross-functional resolution happens within the close window rather than extending it. Treasury operations and accounting work from the same consolidated data, removing the handoff delays that add days to every cycle.


## **Key Takeaways**


The month end close timeline at 50 banks is shaped more by data collection than by accounting complexity. CFOs and controllers should decompose their close into phases and measure how many days are consumed before any actual close work begins. Financial close benchmarks that do not account for banking relationship count are misleading for multi-bank organizations. The most effective way to compress the timeline is not faster reconciliation or more staff. It is eliminating the statement collection phase that delays everything downstream. When every statement is available on day one, a 10-day close becomes a 6-day close without changing any of the accounting work inside it. The days you save are the days you were never doing accounting in the first place.
